Switch those cells on and a mouse freezes with nothing to fear. Switch one type off and learned fear fails.
cards.evidence: single study · mice · single-nucleus RNA sequencing, calcium imaging, in vivo electrophysiology, optogenetics · no sampl

sections.text:
A mouse in a small box hears a tone. It has learned what the tone means: a shock is coming. It stops moving. Not a pause — the whole-body stillness that counts as fear in a mouse, held for as long as the tone plays.

Now look inside its head. For decades the amygdala, a structure deep in the brain, has been called the fear centre. But its neurons do something strange. They fire hard in the first moment of danger, then fall quiet. The alarm rings and stops. The freezing does not.

So what keeps the animal on high alert? Kay Tye's team at the Salk Institute asked it plainly: "what is causing that lingering fear?"

The answer sits where almost nobody had looked. Wedged between two parts of the amygdala, and touching the striatum — the brain's machinery for choosing what to do next — is a thin sliver of tissue called the amygdalostriatal transition zone, or ASt. It is tiny and buried. Researchers were not even sure it was a real region, rather than a blurry border between two famous ones.

The first result is that it is a real place. By reading which genes are switched on inside single cells, the team showed the ASt is genetically unlike both the amygdala and the striatum beside it. A structure, not a seam.

The second result closes the gap. They recorded ASt neurons in freely moving mice while a shock-predicting cue played. Amygdala activity dropped away soon after the threat appeared. ASt activity stayed strong and steady for the whole time the danger lasted.

Then they pushed on it from both sides. Switching ASt neurons on artificially made a mouse freeze and avoid, with no threat in the room. Switching off one group — the cells carrying D2, a docking point for the brain chemical dopamine — broke learned fear: the mouse no longer answered the cue it had been trained on. Enough to cause the behaviour on its own. Needed for it to happen at all.

So the ASt does not just note that something matters. Sitting where emotion meets action, it turns a brief emotional signal into behaviour that holds. Co-author Fergil Mills calls it a missing piece that was "hiding in plain sight".

That reaches past mice. Anxiety disorders, PTSD and panic share one shape: fear that will not switch off once the threat is gone. If noticing danger and staying afraid run through different tissue, a treatment could turn down the part that will not stop — without blinding the part that keeps you alive.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: Three tools, three jobs. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing — reading which genes are active inside single cell nuclei — showed the ASt's cells are unlike their neighbours. Calcium imaging and in vivo electrophysiology, two ways of watching neurons fire inside a living, moving animal, caught the long response to the cue. Optogenetics did the causal work: the neurons are engineered to react to light, so a pulse can switch a chosen group on or shut it off.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is mice, and one study. Freezing at a tone in a box is a clean but narrow model. Human anxiety and PTSD are not that. No animal counts or effect sizes are given here, so how big these effects are is unknown. And the treatment idea comes from the mechanism, not from a finding — nobody has quieted an ASt in a person.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Fear may not be one thing switched on. It may be one part that notices, and another that will not let go.

recall.q: The amygdala's alarm falls quiet early, but the mouse stays frozen. What holds it there, and why does that matter for medicine?
recall.a: The amygdalostriatal transition zone — a small, long-ignored sliver wedged beside the amygdala — keeps firing steadily for as long as the threat lasts. Because starting fear and holding it run through different tissue, a treatment could turn down stuck fear without blinding the brain's first detection of danger.

cards.title: A mouse who gathered sunlight instead of corn
cards.body: In Leo Lionni's 1968 children's book, one field mouse refuses to help store food for the winter. He says he is working anyway — gathering sunlight, colours and words. When the corn runs out and the talk goes flat, the other mice learn what he meant.

sections.text:
The woman on the treadmill has the blank, faraway stare of someone just getting through a workout. She is a physicist. Behind that stare she is working out the logic of black holes. Nobody else in the gym has any idea.

Another scene: a friend on a train, gazing out of the window, doing the slow hidden work that would one day win a Pulitzer Prize — America's biggest award for writing. The theatre director André Gregory once put it this way to the photographer Richard Avedon. Artists are always working, even when they do not look like it. They are like plants in winter. You cannot see the fruit, but something is taking root under the ground.

Leo Lionni built a whole book on that idea and disguised it as a picture book for small children. He fled Holland during the war, settled in America, and made more than forty children's books. Frederick, from 1968, has been called the strongest defence of imagination since the poet William Blake.

A family of field mice lives in a stone wall. Autumn comes and they work day and night, dragging in food for the winter. All of them except one. Frederick stands still and stares at nothing.

They ask him why he doesn't work. "I do work," he says. He is gathering too — sunlight, colours, words, pictures for the mind. Things nobody can eat.

Winter arrives. The mice huddle between the stones, eat well, and chat happily about nothing much. Then the food runs low and the chatter thins out. In the cold and the quiet, someone finally asks Frederick what he gathered.

He tells them to close their eyes, and it works. His words put warmth and colour back into their heads. Then he climbs onto a stone and gives them a verse — "Who scatters snowflakes? Who melts the ice?" — questions nobody can answer, the oldest ones there are. Only now do the mice see that he is a poet, and that he was doing a poet's work all through the hours they thought he was idle.

The book never claims Frederick's gathering is as good as the corn. It lets the winter run long enough to test both, and shows what each one is for. The corn keeps the body going. Frederick keeps something else going — the part of you that can still be interested in being alive, once the eating is done.

The work stays invisible because it can happen in only one place. A poem made of words, a poem made of mathematics: both are built inside a mind, and a mind has no window. The person staring into space on the treadmill, on the train, at the wall, may be the one carrying the winter.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Nobody can watch a mind at work. That is not the same as a mind doing nothing.

recall.q: The other mice ask Frederick why he isn't working. What does he answer, and what does the winter prove about it?
recall.a: He says he is working — gathering sunlight, colours and words instead of corn. When the stored food runs out and the talk goes flat, his poem is the only thing left that helps. Lionni's point: invisible creative work is real provision, not idleness.

cards.title: SEBI's blockchain bond pilot raised ₹1,000 crore
cards.body: The bond and the money now change hands in the same instant, and neither moves without the other. The private keys stay with regulated depositories, so the investor sees nothing new. SEBI, India's markets regulator, calls the pilot Demat 2.0.

sections.text:
The bonds are tokenised. That means each bond is one record several institutions read from, instead of each one keeping its own database and matching them up later.

The bond's terms — coupon dates, interest formula, redemption date — are written in as code, so a payout fires on schedule with no back office cross-checking holders, tax and ledger entries. Cash moves on the RBI's digital rupee (e₹) rails through atomic delivery-versus-payment: bond and money transfer in one go, and if one leg fails, both cancel. That closes the gap where a buyer has paid but has not yet got the bond.

Regulated depositories hold the private keys, so there are no recovery phrases and the usual demat protections still apply.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Over ₹1,000 crore raised by REC, L&T and IIFL Finance combined.
₹1,00,000 of bonds at an 8% yearly coupon pays ₹2,000 every three months — the routine transfer that today needs several middlemen to agree.
Phase 1 of 3 done: issuance only, in a controlled setting.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The Financial Stability Board, which watches the global financial system, flags the cost. Today banks net trades through the day and move only the difference at the end. Settle each trade on its own, the moment it happens, and every institution must keep cash or digital rupees ready upfront for each one. That money sits locked, doing nothing.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The next phase is meant to bring these bonds to the secondary market on existing exchanges, then to retail investors. After that, the network would widen to other regulated bodies such as credit rating agencies.

recall.q: Instant settlement closes one gap for the buyer. What is that gap, and what does closing it cost the banks?
recall.a: The gap is the window where a buyer has paid but has not yet received the bond. Under atomic delivery-versus-payment, bond and money move in one transaction, and if one leg fails, both cancel. The cost: trades no longer net out across the day, so institutions must keep cash or digital rupees ready upfront for every single trade.

cards.title: A plan to contain China, dropped by its own author
cards.body: Noah Smith spent years saying America should handle China the way it handled the Soviet Union: build a huge bloc of allies and wait. He has now dropped that plan. Not because China grew stronger — because America looks too busy fighting itself.

sections.text:
Containment came from George Kennan's 1946 cable from Moscow, the "Long Telegram": assume the rival stays hostile, stay firm, wait for its system to break from inside. Smith's version was economic — tie America to Europe, Japan, Korea and ideally India, a bloc big enough to out-produce China.

That needs an America that stays steady and outward-looking for decades. Trump's presidency, Smith argues, shows the opposite: alliances torn up, and no way back to the old order after he leaves. So the goal shrinks. Not China's collapse, not American supremacy — just keeping smaller countries out from under Beijing's control.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 1946 — Kennan, then acting head of the US embassy in Moscow, sends the telegram that becomes the containment doctrine.
45 years — how long containment ran before the USSR fell.
3 reasons Smith says China is the harder case: far bigger than the USSR, a better economic model, deeply tied into world trade.
Decades — how long America needs to heal its divisions, which is also when China is at its peak relative power.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The new version puts the work on everyone else. Smith says Japanese, Indian, Filipino and Korean people should get to pick their own future, whoever leads the free world. And after Trump's record on detention and threats against other countries, American power no longer automatically means a freer world.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Rush Doshi and Kurt Campbell, two main backers of the allied-bloc strategy, say those alliances could still be rebuilt if America steadies itself believably. The question is whether that happens before China's strongest decades pass.

recall.q: Nothing China did made Smith drop his containment plan. What did?
recall.a: America's own divisions. A country busy fighting itself cannot run a decades-long allied strategy, so Smith gave up the bloc plan — winning now just means stopping China from dominating smaller countries.

cards.title: India's new GDP count leans on tax and company records
cards.body: India is changing how it measures its economy. The new GDP series counts the formal corporate side from paperwork businesses already file. The part that files nothing is measured another way — by survey.

sections.text:
GDP is the total value of everything a country produces. India's statistics ministry says the new series leans far more on records businesses already file: company accounts, GST returns (the goods and services tax that registered businesses file), and filings from limited liability partnerships — a business form sitting between a partnership and a company.

Those records do two jobs. They sharpen the estimate of what private companies produce. They also fix industry classification — deciding which trade a firm belongs to, so its output is counted in the right place.

A large part of India's economy files none of this. Households and unincorporated firms — firms not registered as companies — leave no such paperwork. The ministry measures them directly, through surveys, including labour surveys.

The formal economy read off its paperwork; the rest of it counted by asking.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: A filing is what a business told the tax office. A survey is what someone answered when asked. India's headline growth number now stitches the two together, and it is only as good as both halves.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The ministry has named the sources, not the weights. The figure to look for: how much of GDP now comes from filings, and how much still rests on surveys.

recall.q: The new GDP series measures two parts of the economy in two different ways. What are they?
recall.a: The formal corporate side is built from records businesses already file — company accounts, GST returns, LLP filings. Households and unincorporated firms file nothing, so they are measured directly through surveys.
